articles.summary: The Trump administration on Friday unveiled its America First Seafood Strategy, outlining plans to strengthen the U.S. commercial fishing industry through regulatory reform, investment in fishing vessels and shoreside infrastructure,...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Image credit: NOAA Fisheries The Trump administration on Friday unveiled its America First Seafood Strategy, outlining plans to strengthen the U.S. commercial fishing industry through regulatory reform, investment in fishing vessels and shoreside infrastructure, and tougher enforcement against unfair foreign competition. The strategy , announced October 23, builds on President Donald Trump’s April 2025 executive order, Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness , and brings together several federal agencies to expand domestic seafood production, modernize processing capacity, and improve market access for American fishermen. A major focus is rebuilding the infrastructure that supports the nation’s commercial fishing fleet, including shipyards, docks, cold storage facilities, processing plants, and working waterfronts. Federal agencies will work to streamline permitting and reduce barriers to private investment, while making greater use of existing financing programs administered by NOAA, the Department of Agriculture, and the Small Business Administration. NOAA will also review its Fisheries Finance Program and Capital Construction Fund to identify obstacles that discourage fishermen from replacing aging vessels or investing in safer, more efficient American-built fishing boats. “The America First Seafood Strategy ensures that the future of seafood in the United States will be built by American fishermen, American workers, and American industry—not by foreign imports,” said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. The initiative comes as the administration pursues a broader effort to rebuild America’s maritime industrial base, including domestic shipbuilding capacity and the U.S.-flagged fleet. Beyond infrastructure, the strategy calls for changes to federal fisheries management aimed at increasing sustainable harvests and reducing regulatory costs. NOAA will work with regional fishery management councils and industry representatives to ensure catch limits reflect the best available science, restore access to productive fishing grounds where supported by data, and eliminate compliance requirements that do not contribute to conservation goals. The administration also plans to strengthen the position of American seafood in domestic markets. A proposed voluntary “U.S.-Caught Seafood” designation would help consumers identify products harvested by American fishermen aboard U.S.-flagged vessels operating under U.S. fisheries management. The Food and Drug Administration issued draft guidance Friday outlining how companies could use U.S.-origin statements and labeling. Federal agencies will also seek to expand purchases of American seafood through government procurement programs and launch a nationwide “Eat American Seafood” campaign. On the trade front, the strategy calls for stronger enforcement against illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing, seafood fraud, and mislabeling. NOAA plans to improve its Seafood Import Monitoring Program, using advanced technology and more targeted inspections to identify high-risk imports. The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative will also work with other agencies to address unfair foreign trade practices and improve access to overseas markets for American seafood exporters. Marine aquaculture is another priority, with federal agencies expected to establish clearer permitting standards for operations in federal waters. Notably, the strategy does not announce new federal spending. Instead, it relies on existing programs and statutory authorities, with an emphasis on regulatory changes, interagency coordination, and attracting private investment. NOAA said progress will be measured through increases in domestic seafood production and processing, private capital investment, American jobs supported, and reduced dependence on foreign supply chains. The broader goal is to keep more of the economic value of American seafood in the United States, from vessels harvesting fish offshore to the shipyards, processors, and waterfront businesses that support the industry. articles.title: Shipping community issues clear call for IMO regulation to turn first-mover action into a global transition
articles.summary: Global leaders from across the maritime value chain met in Shanghai this week for the Global Maritime Forum Annual Summit 2026, where much of the discussion centred around the future of shipping’s energy transition. With the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework facing a pivotal point in...
articles.body: Shipping community issues clear call for IMO regulation to turn first-mover action into a global transition in International Shipping News 24/10/2026 Global leaders from across the maritime value chain met in Shanghai this week for the Global Maritime Forum Annual Summit 2026, where much of the discussion centred around the future of shipping’s energy transition. With the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework facing a pivotal point in December, the Summit provided a timely opportunity for decision-makers to engage in crucial conversations about the industry’s green transition. By the end of the two days, a clear message emerged that IMO regulation will be essential to accelerating that transition, with many participants voicing support. Among those present at the Summit was IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez, who spoke about the importance of a global regulatory framework in incentivising the investments the industry needs to reach the IMO’s net-zero targets. “The goal remains in place: the decarbonisation of the sector is by 2050. We still need countries to invest in infrastructure beyond the IMO, and the energy sector to invest in new fuels. The more we diversify, the more resilient we are,” he said. Over the last few days, shipowners, charterers, financiers, policymakers, and cargo owners had a rare chance to speak candidly, test assumptions, and understand each other’s priorities. Conversation topics ranged from decarbonisation and energy security to maritime governance and freedom of navigation, seafarer safety, and supply chain disruption. “The value of a gathering like this is greatest when the stakes are highest, and the shipping industry is currently facing its fair share of challenges,” said Johannah Christensen, CEO of the Global Maritime Forum. “Leaders are facing fundamental dilemmas, like how to continue trading vital goods during times of rupture without risking lives. The Annual Summit 2026 provided an invaluable opportunity for them to come together with peers and discuss a path forward.” New report reveals China’s strengths across green shipping corridor building blocks This year’s Annual Summit, the first to be hosted in mainland China, provided an opportunity not only to connect with key Chinese business leaders and policymakers but also to learn more about China’s progress in the green transition. Launched here in Shanghai, the Global Maritime Forum’s newest report looks at China’s strategic advantages in the four key building blocks considered crucial to successfully starting up a green corridor. ‘Green shipping corridors: How China is re-energising the global movement’ finds that China is one of the strongest actors globally in this space, holding strategic advantages in three of the four building blocks. Swire Shipping CEO Jeremy Sutton announced as new All Aboard Alliance co-chair Also at the Summit, the All Aboard Alliance announced Swire Shipping CEO Jeremy Sutton as its new co-chair, alongside existing co-chair and Circle Digital Ventures CEO Meei Wong. “On behalf of Swire Shipping, it is an honour to be appointed co-chair of the All Aboard Alliance. Creating a safer, more inclusive, and respectful maritime industry is not only the right thing to do, it is essential to the future of shipping,” said Jeremy Sutton, Swire Shipping CEO and new Alliance co-chair. “I look forward to working with Alliance members to build on existing momentum and help create a vibrant maritime sector where everyone has the opportunity to succeed and thrive.” The All Aboard Alliance’s work to develop global standards across ten areas of life at sea was a focal point across many discussions at the Summit. Participants agreed that the project is essential to the industry’s long-term future, particularly given the current context regarding seafarer safety in the Strait of Hormuz. Annual Summit 2027 to be held in Copenhagen In the closing session yesterday, it was announced that the Annual Summit 2027 will be held from 28-29 September in Copenhagen, Denmark. Next year will mark the tenth anniversary of the Global Maritime Forum, which is headquartered in Copenhagen. Denmark’s long maritime history and integral role in the sector makes Copenhagen a natural place to host the tenth Annual Summit. The Annual Summit 2026 was co-hosted by Shanghai Maritime University, with support provided by Summit partners Shanghai International Port Group, the People’s Government of Hongkou District, and Baltic Exchange. “It has been our privilege to host key stakeholders from across the maritime value chain here in Shanghai. This year’s summit serves as a wonderful international exchange opportunity on the latest global shipping practices. We recognise the importance of stabilising market expectations and encouraging collaborative innovation. Shanghai Maritime University will endeavour to foster new forces for shipping development through talent cultivation,” said Professor Beiping Chu, President of Shanghai Maritime University. “As a partner of the Global Maritime Forum Annual Summit 2026, Shanghai International Port Group congratulates the Forum on a successful gathering in Shanghai—a city and port that have long been a gateway for global trade—and the energy and ideas shared here give us confidence that, even amid uncertainty, our industry can work together toward a more resilient and sustainable future,” said Song Xiaodong, President of Shanghai International Port Group. “We look forward to continuing our collaboration with the Global Maritime Forum and all partners. Let us work together to weather the storm, jointly advance the building of a maritime community with a shared future, and shape a greener, more inclusive and sustainable future for global shipping,” said Jie Cao, Deputy Director, Shipping Department of the People’s Government of Hongkou. “This year’s Global Maritime Forum summit in Shanghai was a vital opportunity for the international shipping community to better understand the complexities of modern trade. As volatility and uncertainty for global shipping markets continue, it was important for our industry to come together to share insights and experiences, and for Baltic Exchange to showcase its role in providing independent market benchmarks to help the market make more informed decisions,” said Mark Jackson, CEO of Baltic Exchange. articles.summary: China’s iron ore imports have been on the rise so far in 2026, providing the dry bulk market with the respective tailwinds. articles.body: Dry Bulk Market: China’s Iron Ore Imports on The Rise in Dry Bulk Market , Hellenic Shipping News 24/10/2026 C hina’s iron ore imports have been on the rise so far in 2026, providing the dry bulk market with the respective tailwinds. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Banchero Costa said that “2025 was another positive year for global seaborne iron ore trade. In Jan-Dec 2025, global loadings of iron ore increased by +3.5% y-o-y to 1,732.0 mln tonnes, based on AXS Marine vessel tracking data. 2026 has remained on a positive, albeit slower, note, with export volumes up by +1.0% y-o-y in JanSep 2026 to 1,279.2 mln tonnes. Exports from Australia increased in Jan-Sep 2026 by +2.2% y-o-y to 713.0 mln tonnes. From Brazil, exports declined by -1.5% y-o-y in Jan-Sep 2026 to 284.3 mln t. From Canada there was a -8.0% y-oy decline to 43.7 mln tonnes. From South Africa volumes were essentially flat, -0.1% y-o-y, at 41.0 mln t. India saw an increase of +3.2% y-o-y in Jan-Sep 2026 to 20.1 mln t. From Norway exports increased by +2.2% y-o-y to 16.0 mln t”. According to the shipbroker, “demand is still driven primarily by Mainland China, which accounts for 75% of imports. Iron ore imports into China increased by +4.1% y-o-y in Jan-Sep 2026 to 967.8 mln tonnes. Imports into Japan declined by -3.6% y-o-y to 69.2 mln t. To the EU, imports declined by -3.1% y-o-y to 53.1 mln t. Volumes into South Korea increased by +3.7% y-o-y to 55.3 mln t. Imports into Malaysia increased by +6.2% y-o-y to 19.2 mln tonnes. To Vietnam volumes were up by +20.2% y-o-y to 20.8 mln t. To Oman, volumes were down -22.7% y-o-y to 8.3 mln t, to Saudi Arabia down by -70.6% y-o-y to 2.5 mln t, to Bahrain -78.8% y-o-y to 2.0 mln t”. Banchero Costa said that “mainland China is by far the largest importer of iron ore in the world. China accounted for 74.6% of global iron ore imports in Jan-Dec 2025. Imports into China increased +4.0% y-o-y in Jan-Dec 2024 to 1,256.4 mln tonnes. They have further increased by +1.8% y-o-y in Jan-Dec 2025 to 1,279.4 mln t, which is a new alltime record. As already mentioned, in Jan-Sep 2026, imports into China increased by +4.1% y-o-y to 967.8 mln t. This was driven primarily by a very strong +11.3% y-o-y surge in 1Q26, whilst growth moderated to +1.1% yo-y in 2Q26 and +0.5% y-o-y in 3Q26. The vast majority (71%) of iron ore volumes into China in Jan-Sep 2026 were loaded on Capesizes (130,000- 220,000 dwt), with a further 21% carried on VLOCs (over 220,000 dwt), whilst just 3% was carried on Post-Panamaxes, 2% on Panamaxes, and 3% on Supramaxes. The main iron ore import terminals in Mainland China are: Caofeidian (115.6 mln t discharged in Jan-Sep 2026), Tangshan/Jingtang (91.3 mln t), Lanshan (81.0 mln t), Ningbo/Zhoushan (80.9 mln t), Tianjin (64.1 mln t), Rizhao (58.2 mln t), Lianyungang (57.2 mln t), Dongjiakou (54.4 mln t), Huanghua (45.1 mln t), Fangcheng (39.5 mln t), Zhanjiang (38.8 mln t)”. Meanwhile, “in terms of sources for China’s iron ore imports, Australia remains by far the top source country, with a 62.7% share in Jan-Sep 2026. Iron ore imports from Australia to China in Jan-Sep 2026 have increased by +1.9% y-o-y to an alltime high for the period of 606.5 mln tonnes, from 595.0 mln t in Jan-Sep 2025. The top loading port in Australia for iron ore cargoes to China is Port Hedland (354.2 mln t in Jan-Sep 2026). Brazil remains in second spot with a 21.5% share in Jan-Sep 2026. Imports to China from Brazil increased by +5.1% y-o-y in Jan-Sep 2026 to 208.3 mln tonnes, from 198.2 mln t in Jan-Sep 2025. The top port in Brazil for cargoes to China was Ponta da Madeira (78.2 mln t in Jan-Sep 2026). Volumes from South Africa to China declined by -7.1% y-o-y to 23.4 mln t in Jan-Sep 2026. From India volumes increased by +12.4% y-o-y to 19.4 mln t. From Peru volumes surged by +49.6% y-o-y to 18.5 mln t”, the shipbroker concluded. Nikos Roussanoglou, Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide Tops 2026-10-24 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

2026 has remained on a positive, albeit slower, note, with export volumes up by +1.0% y-o-y in JanSep 2026 to 1,279.2 mln tonnes.

articles.title: Sanctions risks reshape commodity trading
articles.summary: Commodity traders are operating in an increasingly fragmented sanctions environment where geopolitical developments can determine not only whether a transaction is lawful, but whether it can be financed, insured and ultimately completed, according to a briefing from law firm HFW. articles.body: Sanctions risks reshape commodity trading in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 24/10/2026 C ommodity traders are operating in an increasingly fragmented sanctions environment where geopolitical developments can determine not only whether a transaction is lawful, but whether it can be financed, insured and ultimately completed, according to a briefing from law firm HFW. In the briefing, authors Daniel Martin, HFW partner, and Amanda Rathbone, HFW knowledge counsel (commodities) said that sanctions compliance has evolved from a specialist legal consideration into a central strategic concern for commodity businesses trading oil, gas, metals and agricultural products. Martin and Rathbone warn that the sanctions environment is changing so rapidly that risks can evolve significantly during the lifecycle of a single transaction, from initial negotiations through to shipment, financing and payment. As a result, companies are increasingly being forced to reassess traditional compliance processes and adopt broader, more dynamic risk management strategies. For commodity traders, geopolitical risk is no longer something that sits in the background of a transaction, they wrote. “It is much higher on the agenda and for good reason: depending on the jurisdiction, it can determine whether a trade is both permissible and economically viable, whether banks will finance it, whether insurers will cover it and whether the board and shareholders are willing to back it.” They frame today’s sanctions environment as an “odyssey” for international businesses, drawing parallels with the trials faced by the mythical Greek hero Odysseus. Rather than navigating a single obstacle, commodity traders are now confronted with multiple, overlapping challenges that can shift unexpectedly as political priorities change. Widening gap Among the most significant challenges identified in the report is the growing divergence between major sanctions regimes. According to HFW, the US, European Union and the UK are no longer necessarily aligned in their approaches to countries such as Russia and Iran. This divergence has created a complex compliance landscape in which an activity permitted under one jurisdiction’s rules may face restrictions or heightened scrutiny under another’s. “Businesses operating internationally now have to manage several overlapping, sometimes conflicting, sets of restrictions,” the authors note. They add that companies should resist becoming overly reliant on established compliance procedures because “things may have changed, even during the course of a transaction”. The report also highlights how sanctions programmes have expanded beyond their traditional focus on military, dual-use and advanced technology goods. Governments are increasingly using sanctions as instruments of broader geopolitical policy, meaning that ordinary commercial activity and seemingly routine commodity trades can now attract scrutiny. At the same time, countermeasures adopted by other states are adding additional layers of complexity. HFW warns that efforts to comply with one jurisdiction’s sanctions requirements can sometimes increase exposure to conflicting regulations elsewhere, creating difficult commercial and legal dilemmas for international trading businesses. Additionally, when companies based in Europe, the UK or the US withdraw from sanctioned markets, commercial activity often migrates to jurisdictions that have not adopted comparable restrictions. They caution that while the fact that a particular trade “has migrated outside its traditional markets does not, by itself, point to improper activity”… “the potential involvement of participants willing to disguise the true nature of a transaction through intermediaries, opaque corporate structures, unusual trading routes or misleading documentation”. The report recommends that shipping businesses pay close attention to changes in counterparties, routing arrangements, ownership structures, documentation and payment mechanisms, as these can all be indicators of sanctions-related risk. Secondary worries Another area of growing concern is the increasing use of secondary sanctions. Historically, secondary sanctions were designed to influence the behaviour of non-US entities by restricting access to American markets and opportunities. HFW notes that the consequences have become far more severe, particularly given the possibility that non-US companies themselves could become designated sanctions targets. “The commercial calculation can now be considerably starker,” the authors said. “The possibility that a business itself might be designated can operate as an extremely powerful means of changing behaviour outside the sanctioning state’s ordinary jurisdiction.” They add that for international traders, shipowners, insurers and banks, such a designation “may in practice be existential”. The briefing also points to increasing expectations from regulators, who now expect companies to investigate broader sanctions risks throughout a transaction rather than relying solely on screening immediate contractual counterparties against sanctions lists. As sanctions lists continue to grow, traditional screening methods are increasingly strained. Although technology can eliminate many false positives, more complex cases still require detailed human assessment, said HFW. Meanwhile, entities seeking to evade sanctions have become increasingly sophisticated in their methods, creating further pressure on compliance teams. Rather than relying exclusively on list screening, HFW recommends a risk-based compliance approach focused on understanding the substance of each transaction. This includes examining who ultimately controls a counterparty, where goods originate, how they will be transported, which financial and insurance institutions are involved and why a transaction has been structured in a particular manner. The report also advocates bringing sanctions assessments much earlier into the deal-making process. According to the authors, sanctions reviews should no longer be treated as a final-stage compliance exercise but should instead become part of the initial commercial evaluation of an opportunity. “Before committing significant resources to an opportunity, traders need sufficient visibility over the supply chain, counterparties and payment arrangements to decide whether the trade is realistic,” they said. Martin and Rathbone believe sanctions complexity is unlikely to diminish. They identify three major trends that commodity businesses need to understand: continuing divergence between sanctions regimes, greater emphasis on understanding ownership and supply-chain risks rather than simple list screening, and increasing judicial involvement as sanctions-related disputes reach the courts. The authors conclude that sanctions compliance has become a strategic discipline that extends far beyond legal departments and now influences market selection, financing relationships, insurance availability and corporate risk appetite. “There is no obvious end to this particular odyssey,” Martin and Rathbone concluded. Source: Baltic Exchange Tops 2026-10-24 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: As a result, companies are increasingly being forced to reassess traditional compliance processes and adopt broader, more dynamic risk management strategies.
For commodity traders, geopolitical risk is no longer something that sits in the background of a transaction, they wrote.
Rather than navigating a single obstacle, commodity traders are now confronted with multiple, overlapping challenges that can shift unexpectedly as political priorities change.

articles.body: Baltic Dry Index Snaps 4-Day Winning Run in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 24/10/2026 The Baltic Exchange’s dry bulk freight index, which tracks rates for ships carrying dry bulk commodities, snapped its four-day winning streak on Friday, falling by 1.2% to 2,660 points. The panamax index, which usually carries 60,000 to 70,000 tons of coal or grain, dropped roughly 2% to a fresh low since August 24 at 2,109 points. Meanwhile, the capesize index, which typically transports 150,000-ton cargoes, including iron ore and coal, also halted its four-day winning run, decreasing by 1.5% to 3,791 points. Among smaller vessels, the supramax index went down by 0.2% to 1,887 points. For the week, the benchmark index advanced about 5.9%, notching its second consecutive weekly gain, mainly supported by the bigger-size segment. articles.body: What is changing behind dry bulk and tanker freight markets? in International Shipping News 24/10/2026 A longside our weekly Dry and Tanker Market Monitors, this Market Insight presents our Commodity Freight Watch, examining developments that could influence seaborne trade and freight in the coming weeks. While the Monitors assess freight performance and vessel supply, this analysis focuses on the underlying commodity developments shaping cargo availability, supported by Signal Ocean Platform data on shipment patterns, loading activity and vessel deployment. Key factors in dry bulk include Chinese and Indian coal policies, Indonesian export authorizations, iron ore loading delays at Saldanha, and a resurgence in US soybean acquisitions. Meanwhile, oil cargo flows may be shaped by shifting product-export rules and updated sanctions policies, alongside loading schedule risks driven by refinery outages and the Petersburg terminal fire. Ultimately, the location and timing of available cargoes will dictate the near-term freight trajectory. SPOTLIGHT OF THE WEEK | GRAIN US–China Grain: The Shipment Pattern Behind the New Purchases Chinese soybean purchases strengthen the US forward cargo book. USDA reported 558,000 tonnes of soybean sales to China on 16 October, following 330,000 tonnes on 15 October. China-designated sales announced during 14–16 October reached 1.36 million tonnes for the 2026/27 marketing year. Additional sales included 236,000 tonnes of soybeans to unknown destinations and 127,000 tonnes of corn to Japan. These commitments support future US grain export programmes, although their contribution to Panamax and Kamsarmax employment will depend on shipment dates and loading ports. US–China grain shipments recovered in September following a summer slowdown. Signal Ocean Platform data show stronger monthly US–China grain exports during the first five months of 2026 compared with 2025, followed by weaker summer activity and a September rebound. The earlier soybean-specific selection recorded 10.87 million tonnes during January–August, up 86% year on year, before the subsequent recovery in shipments. Panamax vessels account for the largest share of the displayed grain movements, with the US Gulf remaining the principal loading region alongside Pacific coast exports. COAL | POLICY AND QUOTAS RESHAPE ASIAN SUPPLY China is balancing tighter mine-safety oversight with efforts to maintain domestic coal supply ahead of the winter heating season. September raw coal output fell 6.8% y/y to 385 Mt, a decline attributed in reporting to stricter safety inspections after the May accident in Shanxi and a fatal accident in Hunan in August. On 16 October, the NDRC and the National Energy Administration urged Shanxi to bring idled mines back into operation and raise output before winter. India continues to prioritise domestic coal production and rail distribution to power plants. The Ministry of Coal reported average daily supply to the power sector rising from 2.2 Mt in September to 2.5 Mt over 1–10 October, with rail loading up from 426 to 469 rakes per day. The Power Secretary ruled out a mandatory imported-coal blending requirement for power plants this year. Indonesia 2027 coal production quotas under review: Indonesia opened applications for its 2027 production plans (RKAB) on 1 October, with submissions due by 15 November. The government is assessing production allocations, while uncertainty over approved volumes has already slowed negotiations for 2027 coal supply contracts. For the dry bulk freight market, the outcome will be important for Indonesian export commitments and prospective coal cargo availability across Asian routes. IRON ORE AND GRAIN | SUPPLY RISKS Iron ore – Saldanha terminal reaches scheduled maintenance deadline. South Africa’s Saldanha Iron Ore Terminal is scheduled to complete its 16-day maintenance programme on 21 October, following repairs to shiploaders, conveyors and rail tipplers. Separately, maintenance on the Sishen–Saldanha railway was scheduled to conclude on 16 October. With the terminal handling more than 50 million tonnes of iron ore annually, Capesize employment will focus on resuming loading operations and timing export cargoes after the shutdown. Transnet’s longer-term investment in rail and terminal infrastructure aims to improve the reliability of South Africa’s iron ore export corridor. Grain – wheat supply shifts and stronger U.S. corn export prospects. USDA’s October outlook points to tighter global wheat trade and stronger U.S. corn export prospects for 2026/27. Reduced wheat export availability from Russia and the United States, partly offset by Argentina and Canada, places greater importance on where importers secure their cargoes. Black Sea disruptions add pressure to sourcing decisions, particularly for buyers in North Africa and Asia. Grain – Black Sea attacks intensify pressure on Ukraine’s export corridors. Maritime security risks escalated in mid-October after HS Dignity sank and Chelsea 3 was damaged in reported drone attacks off Bulgaria on 13 October. Russia subsequently claimed strikes on Ukraine’s Izmail port and commercial vessels on 15 October, although these claims remain independently unverified. Ukraine’s grain and pulse exports reached 5.44 million tonnes by 7 October, down 24% year on year, with wheat shipments falling 42%. Worsening Black Sea security has increased reliance on alternative export corridors, particularly the Danube route through Izmail, Reni and Romania’s Constanța, while Baltic ports are also being explored. Congestion at the Sulina Canal has added to the pressure, with vessel waiting times previously exceeding two weeks. The European Council called on 16 October for the restoration of safe commercial navigation and further support for the EU–Ukraine Solidarity Lanes. For Handysize and smaller bulk carriers, the shift towards alternative loading ports, longer waiting times and higher freight costs is changing voyage economics, although additional corridor capacity remains constrained by security risks and inland logistics bottlenecks. OIL | CRUDE FLOWS IN FOCUS Crude Trade Geography: Shifting Origin and Loading-Port Shares Geopolitical disruptions are reshaping the geography of seaborne crude trade, with changes in supply origins, loading terminals and destination markets becoming more pronounced in 2026. Signal Ocean data highlights a greater share of crude originating from Russia, the UAE and the United States, alongside a shift in loading activity towards Fujairah and away from Ras Tanura and Basrah. On the demand side, India’s share has increased while China’s has declined. 2025 – Saudi Arabia held the largest share of seaborne crude origins at 13.6%, ahead of Russia (10.9%) and the United States (8.3%). China accounted for 22.9% of destinations, more than twice India’s 10.6% share. At the loading-port level, Ras Tanura led with 11.3%, reflecting the importance of Saudi export infrastructure in the distribution of crude cargoes. 2026 – A different supply ranking and a shift in loading geography. Russia (12.3%) and the UAE (11.0%) have moved ahead of Saudi Arabia (10.3%) in the January–September origin distribution, while Iraq’s share has fallen from 7.5% to 3.6%. The most pronounced change is at the loading-port level: Fujairah’s share has risen from 2.8% to 9.2%, overtaking Ras Tanura, whose share has declined from 11.3% to 4.0%. This redistribution is particularly relevant for tanker deployment, as greater loading activity outside the Strait of Hormuz changes where vessels need to position for their next cargo. On the destination side, China remains the largest market, although its share has declined from 22.9% to 17.6%, while India’s has increased from 10.6% to 11.8%. OIL | REGULATORY ENVIRONMENT Crude and fleet Graham Act waiver. The 16 October US executive order implementing the Graham Act waived specified new sanctions and duties, including the additional 100% duty on new purchases of Russian-origin crude oil and natural gas by the five largest importers from 18 October. The waivers remain in effect until the President or the Secretary of State decides further action is appropriate; sanctions under earlier executive orders remain in force. Sanctioned-tanker sales – under consideration. US officials have outlined a possible route for legitimate buyers to acquire sanctioned tankers, subject to OFAC authorisation and removal of vessel sanctions on a case-by-case basis, for employment in non-sanctioned trades.OFAC’s public notices reviewed through 20 October did not identify a general authorisation or vessel delistings implementing the initiative. The implications for tanker supply depend on how many vessels secure approval and return to commercial service, and when. Until those steps are confirmed, the initiative cannot be treated as an increase in available tonnage or evidence of freight relief. Oil products Russian diesel exports resume, with first US-bound shipment scheduled. The US licence issued on 9 October, alongside Russia’s partial easing of its diesel export ban from 10 October, has opened the way for additional Russian diesel shipments. The first confirmed export movement involved approximately 40,000 tonnes of ultra-low sulphur diesel loaded at Primorsk on 13 October, bound for Morocco. On 21 October, Russia announced plans to dispatch its first US-bound diesel cargo of 40,000 tonnes on 22 October, with further shipments expected. The US exemption covers specified Russian-origin diesel transactions until 7 April 2027, but does not extend to crude oil. For product tankers, the resumption introduces additional cargo opportunities from Russian export terminals, with the destination mix and pace of subsequent loadings determining the impact on vessel employment and tonne-mile demand. India – lower diesel export duty improves shipment economics. Effective 16 October, India reduced the special additional excise duty on diesel exports from INR 16 to INR 8.5 per litre, while increasing the petrol export duty from INR 0.5 to INR 2.5 per litre. The jet-fuel duty remained unchanged at INR 10.5 per litre. The reduction lowers the tax burden on diesel exports and could encourage additional overseas sales, subject to refinery output, domestic requirements and international demand. China – October fuel export approvals support renewed shipments. Beijing reportedly approved approximately 3.7 million tonnes of diesel, gasoline and jet-fuel exports for October following the Golden Week holiday. These approvals provide scope for Chinese refiners to resume overseas sales, although the volume represents reported export authorisations rather than confirmed shipments. The pace of cargo nominations and loading activity will determine the additional product tanker demand. IEA – Diesel stock releases add to available supply. On 15 October, the International Energy Agency outlined plans to accelerate the release of remaining emergency stocks, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel. The additional supply could help meet immediate product requirements, although the impact on seaborne trade will depend on where inventories are released and whether buyers source replacement cargoes internationally. Easing export restrictions in Russia, lower diesel export duties in India and new Chinese export approvals improve the outlook for clean petroleum product shipments. IEA stock releases, however, may limit immediate import demand in receiving markets. OIL | DISRUPTIONS AND RECOVERY Crude US Gulf – Offshore production recovery supports export availability. US offshore oil shut-ins declined from 1.46 million b/d on 9 October to 329,059 b/d on 13 October, equivalent to 16.1% of Gulf production. By 14 October, approximately 202,000 b/d (9.9%) remained offline. EIA data released on 15 October showed US commercial crude inventories falling by 8.6 million barrels in the week ended 9 October. The restoration of offshore output improves the supply outlook for US Gulf crude exports, although additional tanker demand will depend on refinery requirements, export nominations and confirmed loadings. Saudi Arabia – Houthi attack raises security concerns at Shaybah oilfield. On 21 October, Saudi authorities reported intercepting a drone targeting Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield. Falling debris reportedly caused a fire outside the processing facility, killing two workers, but oilfield operations were not disrupted. The incident adds to security concerns surrounding Saudi energy infrastructure without establishing a reduction in crude production or exports. Oil products Ryazan refinery – Partial processing disruption following drone attack. The 15 October attack forced the shutdown of Ryazan’s CDU-6 crude distillation unit, with an estimated processing capacity of 160,000 b/d, accounting for almost half the refinery’s total capacity. Three other crude distillation units remained operational, limiting the extent of the disruption. No confirmed restart of CDU-6 has been reported, while the impact on diesel production and export volumes remains unquantified. Petersburg Oil Terminal. Fire raises uncertainty over Baltic product shipments. A drone attack overnight on 18 October caused a fire at Petersburg Oil Terminal, a Baltic export facility handling gasoil, jet fuel, fuel oil and vacuum gasoil. The city governor confirmed the fire, while the extent of damage to loading infrastructure and any interruption to export operations remains unclear. No confirmed cargo cancellations or quantified export losses have been established. Any restrictions on terminal operations could delay product loadings and affect vessel turnaround times, with the freight impact dependent on the duration of the disruption and subsequent cargo schedules. US Gulf production recovery improves crude availability, while attacks on Russian energy infrastructure raise uncertainty over Baltic product shipments despite the easing of diesel export restrictions. KEY TAKEAWAY Recent developments highlight how freight conditions can tighten without a corresponding increase in cargo volumes. Disruptions to loading schedules, port operations and export programmes can delay vessel turnaround and temporarily reduce available tonnage. In a market where cargo flows and vessel positioning are changing rapidly, operational efficiency is becoming an important factor in short-term freight performance, alongside underlying supply-demand fundamentals. Source: By Maria Bertzeletou, Senior Market Analyst, Signal Group, https://www.thesignalgroup.com/newsroom/market-insights-commodity-freight-watch Tops 2026-10-24 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Key factors in dry bulk include Chinese and Indian coal policies, Indonesian export authorizations, iron ore loading delays at Saldanha, and a resurgence in US soybean acquisitions.
Meanwhile, oil cargo flows may be shaped by shifting product-export rules and updated sanctions policies, alongside loading schedule risks driven by refinery outages and the Petersburg terminal fire.
Ultimately, the location and timing of available cargoes will dictate the near-term freight trajectory.

articles.title: The Week in Alt Fuels: The methanol bunker footprint
articles.summary: Methanol bunkering has spread across Europe, Asia and parts of North America, with more ports, physical suppliers and bunker vessels coming into the picture. Several methanol bunker locations have been established in Europe. TankMatch and UniBarge are among the physical suppliers supporting deliveries in the...
articles.body: The Week in Alt Fuels: The methanol bunker footprint in International Shipping News 24/10/2026 Methanol bunkering has spread across Europe, Asia and parts of North America, with more ports, physical suppliers and bunker vessels coming into the picture. Several methanol bunker locations have been established in Europe. TankMatch and UniBarge are among the physical suppliers supporting deliveries in the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) region. Methanol bunker operations have been reported at Gothenburg, Hamburg and Immingham. Bremerhaven and Kiel have demonstrated varying levels of readiness through early operations and trials. Some suppliers like Repsol and Mureloil are ready to offer physical methanol deliveries at Spanish ports, including Bilbao, Mugardos and Barcelona. A particularly broad network of ports has developed across Asia, with methanol bunker operations becoming more common. Several ports across China have hosted methanol bunkering, including Shanghai, Ningbo-Zhoushan, Guangzhou, Qingdao, Dalian and Shenzhen. Suppliers including CIMC Enric, SIPG Energy and China Marine Bunker offer ship-to-ship deliveries across Chinese ports. Activity has also extended to Hong Kong, where Sinopec and Chimbusco Pan Nation have supplied bio-methanol. Elsewhere in Asia, methanol bunkering has been conducted at Busan and Ulsan in South Korea, and Japanese ports including Yokohama and Kinoe. The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) has issued five-year methanol bunker licences to PetroChina, Golden Island and Global Energy Trading that have been effective since January. But the MPA reported no methanol bunker sales in September, extending the streak to seven consecutive months. The Port of Houston in the US hosted a ship-to-ship methanol bunker operation in March, with 2,000 mt of methanol delivered to Tangier Maersk. This was preceded by a barge-to-ship operation in April 2023, when the tankers Stena Pro Marine and Stena Prosperous, owned by the Proman Stena Bulk joint venture, took a total of 2,600 mt of methanol from a Kirby barge. The vessels behind the deliveries The number of bunker barges and chemical tankers capable of carrying methanol and offering ship-to-ship bunkering at these ports has also grown steadily over the years. Golden Centaurus, Golden Antares, Golden Sirius, Anna Cosulich and Vanda Pioneer are among the vessels capable of carrying out methanol bunker deliveries in Singapore. China’s supply network includes Daqing 268, Zhongran Green Energy 85and Jia Chen 17, serving different parts of the country’s coastal bunker market. European operations have involved Evidence and Chicago around the ARA region, Odyssee in northwestern Europe, Bahía Candela in Spain and Nore around Gothenburg and Skaw. Japan’s Eika Maru has supported methanol bunkering at Yokohama. In the US, the barge Kirby 29067 has delivered methanol to Tangier Maersk. Many of these vessels also supply biofuels or conventional bunkers, so being able to deliver methanol does not mean they are always available to do so. The next wave of ports Many other ports are preparing for future methanol demand. VO Chidambaranar, Mumbai and Kandla in India, Seattle, Tacoma, Long Beach and South Louisiana in the US, and Auckland in New Zealand are among the ports exploring or developing methanol bunker capabilities over the next couple of years, although their levels of progress vary considerably. Port authorities in Dhofar in Oman, and Algeciras and Valencia in Spain, have also discussed developing methanol bunker capabilities, but have yet to announce timelines. The overall geographical spread shows that methanol bunkering is moving towards a broader network of potential supply locations. The next challenge is turning that geographical reach into dependable availability, so that ships can obtain methanol not simply where it has been bunkered before, but where and when they actually need it. In other alt fuels news this week, the Zero Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance (ZEMBA) has delivered 82,000 mtCO2-equivalent (mtCO2e) in emissions reductions in 2025 and 2026 under its first low-emission shipping tender with Hapag-Lloyd, which concluded this month. South Korean shipping firm HMM has ordered eight 13,000 TEU LNG-capable container ships from HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and HD Hyundai Samho for delivery from 2029. The vessels will be deployed on its Far East-India-Mediterranean service, HMM said. Danish operator Maersk Tankers plans to retrofit up to 10 very large ammonia carriers (VLACs) with ammonia dual-fuel engines, but said the final decision will “depend on securing commercial commitments from customers”. Source: By Konica Bhatt, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news/ 2026-10-24 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Several methanol bunker locations have been established in Europe.
TankMatch and UniBarge are among the physical suppliers supporting deliveries in the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) region.
Methanol bunker operations have been reported at Gothenburg, Hamburg and Immingham.

articles.title: GMS Week 43 – Freight Refuses to Stay Down
articles.summary: Last week’s dry freight retreat appeared to offer recycling buyers the opening they had been waiting for. It did not last. The Baltic Dry Index recovered from 2,545 on October 15 to 2,693 on Thursday, October 22, led by improving Capesize earnings. Although still below earlier October levels, the recovery has...
articles.body: GMS Week 43 – Freight Refuses to Stay Down in Weekly Demolition Reports 24/10/2026 Last week’s dry freight retreat appeared to offer recycling buyers the opening they had been waiting for. It did not last. The Baltic Dry Index recovered from 2,545 on October 15 to 2,693 on Thursday, October 22, led by improving Capesize earnings. Although still below earlier October levels, the recovery has restored some confidence in continued trading. For recyclers hoping that softer freight would finally release ageing bulkers, the window of opportunity has already narrowed. The energy market supplied a more worrying development. Renewed Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia heightened concerns over Middle Eastern oil supplies, prompting Saudi Aramco to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters on Thursday. Brent climbed above USD 115 per barrel intraday on Friday, its highest level since early May, while WTI moved above USD 100. With Gulf shipping risks and elevated insurance costs continuing to disrupt normal trading patterns, ageing tankers still have compelling reasons to remain employed rather than head for recycling. Dry bulk’s recovery was uneven. Capesizes strengthened to 3,848, while Supramaxes advanced to 1,890. Panamaxes, however, retreated to 2,151, illustrating the different pressures facing individual vessel segments. The broader message remains unchanged: freight earnings and second-hand alternatives continue to discourage owners from releasing sufficient recycling candidates. One week’s decline was encouraging. Its partial reversal has reminded buyers how quickly that encouragement can disappear. Steel markets offered little common direction. Indian plate strengthened during the week, while Bangladesh, Pakistan and China remained unchanged. Domestic finished-steel consumption continues to disappoint across much of the sub-continent, limiting the benefit of otherwise stable steel quotations. Turkey weakened marginally against the international market, although its central bank reduced interest rates from 37% to 36%, offering modest financing relief amid continued currency pressure. Physical waterfront activity nevertheless continued. Alang received additional general cargo and reefer tonnage, Chattogram completed several smaller vessel deliveries, and Gadani welcomed another previously secured bulker. These movements sustain yard operations without signalling a corresponding improvement in fresh recycling sales. The distinction remains important: ships are reaching the beaches, but the next pipeline is still far from full. Bangladesh continues to display the strongest conventional buying appetite, although suitable candidates remain scarce. Pakistan retains healthy underlying demand with greater purchasing discipline, while India continues to benefit from specialist opportunities and improving local steel. Turkey remains cautious as weak domestic consumption restricts further buying enthusiasm. The final quarter is therefore developing much as it began, with buyers seeking tonnage that owners have little urgency to release. Freight has recovered, steel offers mixed support, and recycling demand remains largely intact. The beaches are ready for more business. The ships, for now, still have other plans. articles.title: Seafarers face widening competency gap as digital shipping accelerates, recent research finds
articles.summary: Eighty two per cent of maritime professionals surveyed say current training does not adequately prepare crews for the realities of modern, digitally-enabled vessel operations. Just 18% believe training keeps pace, according to new research from OneOcean and Thetius. Seafarer training is falling behind rapidly...
articles.body: Seafarers face widening competency gap as digital shipping accelerates, recent research finds in International Shipping News 24/10/2026 Eighty two per cent of maritime professionals surveyed say current training does not adequately prepare crews for the realities of modern, digitally-enabled vessel operations. Just 18% believe training keeps pace, according to new research from OneOcean and Thetius. Seafarer training is falling behind rapidly evolving operational realities at sea, according to two new reports commissioned by OneOcean and conducted by maritime innovation consultancy Thetius. The research draws on survey data and interviews with maritime professionals across shipboard and shore-based roles. Those interviewed and surveyed include masters, officers, engineers, superintendents, training personnel, crewing staff, and shore-based operators. Findings reveal two interconnected challenges – that seafarers work in increasingly complex digital environments, and that maritime professionals do not feel well prepared to keep pace with this change. The reports suggest that whilst the global seafaring workforce may be qualified on paper, it is under prepared in practice. According to the first report, Competent or Compliant?, the research found that: 82% of respondents say current training models do not prepare crews for modern operations 52% report that qualified crew struggle in real operations ‘often’ or ‘very often’ 56% say ‘tick box’ compliance contributes to this gap 18% believe current training adequately prepares crews for operational reality The maritime professionals that responded say these competence ‘gaps’ are most visible during: Abnormal or unexpected situations (67%) High-pressure operations (56%) Working between different vessels (36%) When using complex digital systems, ECDIS or reporting tools (31%) According to the second report, Decision-optimised or overloaded? the digital revolution has introduced novel risks alongside new capabilities because the technology can redistribute rather than eliminate work. Modern vessels are highly connected digital ecosystems, and while this has improved reporting, transparency and efficiency, it has also had introduced challenges. Crews increasingly act as the link between systems that do not communicate with one another, manually reconciling conflicting data across displays. The report also found that alert fatigue is a growing risk. For example, following Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) interference, 75% of mariners reported a moderate to significant increase in workload, showing how quickly information overload can escalate when further systems alarm at once. The report suggests that more data does not necessarily lead to better decisions, particularly in high-pressure situations, yet training courses do not sufficiently prepare seafarers to handle this reality. Alex Mangan, Chief Marketing and Communications Officer, OneOcean, said: “Change in shipping will only accelerate as vessels adopt new digital systems to manage tightening international regulation and to sail more efficiently and productively. “This has created a growing gap between the training seafarers receive and the challenges they face at sea. The problem is twofold, coming from rapid technological changes at sea, and from the ways in which training is delivered to crews. Closing this reality gap requires the industry to shift its approaches to competence, to reflect real-world operations.” Nick Chubb, Founder of Thetius, said: “The findings reveal a clear reality gap between the demands of modern shipping and the way competence is developed. As vessels become more digitally complex, the industry must move beyond compliance-based training and equip seafarers with the skills they need to operate safely and effectively.” OneOcean’s own product suite reflects this thinking. The Ocean Learning Platform (OLP) gives operators fleet-wide visibility into crew readiness, turning certification records and assessments into a verified picture of who’s ready, where training gaps remain and, crucially, painting a clear picture of competence levels. OneOcean remains committed to investing in Human Capital Management and empowering continuous workforce planning, development and engagement through digital tools. Both reports were launched via a two-part webinar series hosted by Thetius, featuring live discussion of the findings with industry panellists. The reports and the webinar recordings are available at https://www.oneocean.com/insights/oneocean-thetius-thought-leadership . OneOcean continued the conversation this week at Seatrade Maritime Crew Connect Global’s where Capt. Sanjeev Mathur, SVP, OneOcean, moderated a peer exchange focussed on ‘The Deployment Gap: What the Officer Shortage Actually Costs to Manage’, John Butler, SVP, Technical Ship Management, OneOcean, discussed ‘The Fatigue Timebomb & Shore Leave Erosion: A Witness Stand’ and Anna Ruszczynska – Regional Director – APAC, OneOcean, debated ‘The 800,000 — Who Owns the Race to Train the Guinea Pig Generation?’. Source: OneOcean 2026-10-24 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.summary: Changes between the second quarter and the third quarter of 2026: • HSFO sales up by 50,000 mt to 755,000 mt • VLSFO sales up by 73,000 mt to 427,000 mt • MGO sales up by 18,000 mt to 349,000 mt • ULSFO sales up by 42,000 mt to 165,000 mt • LNG sales down ...
articles.body: Rotterdam’s conventional bunker sales rebound 10% from previous quarter in Port News 24/10/2026 Changes between the second quarter and the third quarter of 2026: • HSFO sales up by 50,000 mt to 755,000 mt • VLSFO sales up by 73,000 mt to 427,000 mt • MGO sales up by 18,000 mt to 349,000 mt • ULSFO sales up by 42,000 mt to 165,000 mt • LNG sales down by 26,000 mt to 97,000 mt • No grey methanol sales Bunker suppliers in Rotterdam sold 1.8 million mt of conventional marine fuels in the third quarter of this year, up 10% from the second quarter, according to data from Port of Rotterdam. Volumes in the second quarter of this year had fallen to their lowest level since the port’s records began in 2010. Conventional fuels sales’ share as a percentage of the port’s total bunker sales rose to 92% in the third quarter, from 87% in the second quarter. Fuel oil grades lead recovery HSFO remained Rotterdam’s best-selling conventional fuel grade, accounting for 42% of conventional bunker sales, and 39% of total sales. HSFO sales rose 7% from the previous quarter to 755,000 mt. VLSFO sales jumped 21% from the previous quarter to 427,000 mt, the grade’s steepest quarterly gain since 2021. VLSFO accounted for 24% of conventional bunker sales. ULSFO sales surged 34% from the previous quarter to 165,000 mt, also its steepest quarterly gain since 2021. The grade made up 9% of conventional fuel sales. MGO sales rose 5% from the previous quarter to 349,000 mt, accounting for 19% of conventional fuel sales. Nine-month sales well below last year Rotterdam’s conventional bunker sales fell 26% year-on-year to 5.1 million mt in the first nine months of 2026, from 6.9 million mt in the same period last year. VLSFO sales dropped the most, falling 42% to 1.2 million mt. HSFO sales declined 21% to 2.1 million mt. LNG bucking the trend LNG bunker sales fell 21% from the previous quarter to 97,000 mt. LNG’s share of Rotterdam’s total bunker sales slipped to 5%, from 7% in the second quarter. LNG sales dropped 35% in the third quarter, compared to the same quarter last year. Rotterdam recorded 324,000 mt of LNG sales in the first three quarters, down 10% compared to the same period last year. articles.summary: The Maritime Administration (MARAD) recently embraced VCM when procuring a new generation of training ships for five of the six state maritime academies. To date, MARAD contractor TOTE Services has delivered four of the five vessels.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network The NSMV II, named Patriot State. Photo courtesy Philly Shipyard By Ira Breskin BRONX, NY — Vessel Construction Management practices received praise at the Shipbuilding in America conference here this week. Vessel Construction Management (VCM) essentially outsources oversight of a ship’s entire construction process, from design to delivery, to a third party acting as the owner’s representative. The vessel construction manager takes charge of the entire project, from procuring materials to testing the vessel before delivery. The Maritime Administration (MARAD) recently embraced VCM when procuring a new generation of training ships for five of the six state maritime academies. To date, MARAD contractor TOTE Services has delivered four of the five vessels. “The goal is to deliver a newbuild ship on time and on budget by reducing direct government involvement with the yard and making the construction process more commercial than normal government procurement,” said Charlie Papavizas, an attorney with Winston Taylor in Washington, D.C. The next challenge is to expand the use of VCM in commercial shipbuilding, said Chris Clark, vice president of new construction at TOTE Services, during the conference. The conference was held earlier this week at the State University of New York Maritime College. Empire State VII, the school’s new training ship, was the first in the series to be delivered on time and within budget by TOTE, arriving in September 2023. TOTE Services is also using VCM practices in two subsequent government projects: the construction of missile range instrumentation vessels and a new class of medium landing ships for the Navy. Several ship operators and ship management companies offer VCM services, with the scope of those services depending on each firm’s expertise. VCM relies on commercial shipbuilding best practices and commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) components rather than military-specification parts, both of which can reduce vessel costs and speed delivery. Moreover, the use of VCM minimizes unnecessary design changes and the resulting change orders, which are often a source of costly contract disputes. articles.title: China Militia Boats Expand 'Battlefield Prep', says Taiwan
articles.summary: China is combining militia vessels with coast guard ships to expand "battlefield preparation" around Taiwan and into the western Pacific, Taiwan's Coast Guard said, warning the operations were also putting pressure on Japan and the Philippines.Responding…
articles.body: China Militia Boats Expand 'Battlefield Prep', says Taiwan Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 Copyright TomKorcak/AdobeStock China is combining militia vessels with coast guard ships to expand "battlefield preparation" around Taiwan and into the western Pacific, Taiwan's Coast Guard said, warning the operations were also putting pressure on Japan and the Philippines. Responding to a Reuters exclusive this month on the first known sighting of a Chinese militia boat off Taiwan's Pacific coast in mid-August, the coast guard said it had dispatched a patrol boat to drive away the vessel, which was operating alongside a Chinese coast guard ship and a research vessel. The coast guard confirmed details in the Reuters report, identifying the suspected militia fishing boat as Minfudingyu 07902 , and said it had come as close as about 2.7 nautical miles outside Taiwan's restricted waters on August 16. China has increased such activity since June in overlapping economic waters involving Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, the coast guard said, after Tokyo and Manila announced talks on maritime boundary delimitation in their exclusive economic zones. EEZs extend 200 nautical miles from the coast and give a coastal state rights to exploit, conserve and manage natural resources in those waters. "Such complex grey-zone operations not only increase the maritime surveillance and response burden on Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, but may also create regional security pressure and affect the existing international maritime order," Taiwan's Coast Guard said in a statement to Reuters. China's defence ministry, and the Philippines defence and foreign ministries did not immediately respond to requests for comment.Japan's coast guard declined immediate comment. The coast guard said the vessels' coordinated activity was part of a broader pattern of Chinese "grey-zone" operations using law-enforcement, scientific and civilian cover to expand Beijing's influence at sea while remaining below the threshold of open conflict. The Chinese operations were aimed at "assisting 'battlefield preparation'," the coast guard said, adding Taiwan's east coast was an important maritime traffic and supply route and that continued Chinese activity there could further increase security pressure on Taiwan. Officials in Taiwan say they believe China is practicing for a possible maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets. China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has not ruled out the use of force to achieve its goals. Taiwan's government rejects the claim and says only the island's people can decide their future. China has repeatedly said its operations off Taiwan's east coast are "legitimate and lawful" because they are in Chinese waters, a position Taipei's government strongly rejects. Taiwan's coast guard said it had placed the Minfudingyu 07902 on a priority watchlist, assessing the boat showed the "characteristics" of Chinese maritime militia activity and said it would continue tracking the vessel. Dating back to the 1950s, China's maritime militia uses fishing vessels with trained, state-supported crews to operate in disputed waters, often alongside coast guard ships around South China Sea flashpoints, helping Beijing assert maritime claims while maintaining a civilian appearance. The surveillance report reviewed by Reuters was conducted by Taiwan's Apex Aviation, which used radar screenshots, infrared imagery and automatic-identification system data from a reconnaissance flight to document the cluster of vessels. (Reuters)

articles.summary: The Trump administration is proposing to extend its suspension of port fees targeting China-linked vessels for another two months, pushing their potential return into January 2027 as Washington and Beijing...

REUTERS/Carlos Barria/File Photo The Trump administration is proposing to extend its suspension of port fees targeting China-linked vessels for another two months, pushing their potential return into January 2027 as Washington and Beijing continue negotiations over China’s dominance of global shipbuilding. The proposal, outlined in a Federal Register notice scheduled for publication October 26, would extend the existing one-year suspension through January 9, 2027. The current pause is set to expire November 9. The extension would provide another reprieve for shipping companies facing potentially significant fees on Chinese-owned, Chinese-operated and Chinese-built vessels calling at U.S. ports, as well as certain foreign-built vehicle carriers. “The United States is continuing to engage with China with the goal of obtaining the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices at issue in the investigation,” USTR said in the notice. Under the proposal, the measures would remain suspended from November 10, 2026, through January 9, 2027. During that period, shipping companies would not incur liability for port fees under Annexes I, II and III of the original Section 301 action. The suspension would also continue to cover certain duties on ship-to-shore cranes and cargo-handling equipment. The proposed extension comes nearly a year after President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to suspend the port fees as part of a broader trade agreement reached in South Korea. Washington began collecting the fees on October 14, 2025, but suspended them on November 10, meaning the measures were in effect for less than four weeks. China also suspended its retaliatory fees on U.S.-linked vessels. The original measures emerged from a Section 301 investigation launched during the Biden administration following a 2024 petition by the United Steelworkers and other labor organizations. The investigation concluded that China’s industrial policies and subsidies distorted global competition and undermined U.S. commerce. The resulting port fees became a central part of the Trump administration’s strategy to counter China’s maritime dominance and encourage investment in American shipbuilding. Growing Pressure to Reinstate Fees The latest proposal comes despite mounting pressure from some lawmakers and maritime labor groups to bring the fees back. In June, Senators Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) urged the administration to immediately reinstate the measures , arguing that their suspension undermined efforts to rebuild the U.S. commercial shipbuilding industry. “Section 301 port fees are critical to revitalizing U.S. shipbuilding,” the senators wrote in a letter to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The lawmakers pointed to China’s growing share of global shipbuilding, noting that Chinese yards now account for more than half of global commercial vessel production, compared with just 0.1% for the United States. They also questioned whether Washington had secured meaningful concessions from Beijing in exchange for suspending the fees and how the administration intended to fund its proposed Maritime Security Trust Fund without the revenue. Maritime labor unions have similarly criticized the suspension, arguing that it weakens one of the few measures specifically designed to counter China’s state-supported shipbuilding industry. Shipping companies, meanwhile, have welcomed the reprieve. The original fees threatened to impose substantial costs on carriers and disrupt established shipping networks. During the brief period the measures were active, U.S. carrier Matson reported incurring $6.4 million in reciprocal Chinese port fees, while China’s state-owned COSCO faced an estimated $1.5 billion in annual U.S. charges. Andy Abbott, CEO of ACL, told gCaptain that any port fees would impact its growing US export business, and customers are concerned ACL. “ACL’s unique ships were mistakenly classified by USTR as vehicle carriers even though only 1% of its cargo is automobiles,” explained Abbott. “Our largest US container and heavy machinery customers were panicking that we would redeploy our ships out of the US trade to the booming China trade. This development allows us to continue serving the US market with the fastest transit times from the US East Coast to Europe.” The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) and World Shipping Council both welcomed last year’s suspension, warning that the competing U.S. and Chinese measures risked increasing transportation costs and disrupting global trade. A Broader Debate Over Port Fees The proposed extension also comes as the administration considers a much broader port fee system under its Maritime Action Plan , unveiled earlier this year. Unlike the China-specific Section 301 measures, the plan envisions fees on all foreign-built commercial vessels calling at U.S. ports, with proceeds supporting domestic shipbuilding through a proposed Maritime Security Trust Fund. The plan outlined potential fees ranging from 1 cent to 25 cents per kilogram of imported cargo, which the administration estimated could generate as much as $1.5 trillion over 10 years at the upper end. ICS has warned that such broad-based charges could significantly increase shipping costs and disrupt global trade, even as it supports efforts to expand U.S. shipbuilding capacity. The proposals underscore the competing pressures facing the administration as it seeks to revive American shipyards without imposing additional costs on U.S. importers, exporters and consumers. For now, the latest USTR proposal would leave the China-specific port fee measures on hold for another two months, while negotiations continue. USTR has opened a public comment period on the extension, with submissions due by 5 p.m. Eastern Time on October 30. Comments can be filed through the USTR public comment portal under docket USTR-2026-0694. The extension has not yet been finalized. The notice also does not address whether China will extend its own suspension of retaliatory fees on U.S.-linked vessels. articles.title: Record Tanker Rates Threaten to Push U.S. Oil Exports to Asia to Seven-Year Low
articles.summary: US crude oil exports to Asia are set to hit multi-year lows after the Iran war disrupted global shipping and pushed the cost to lease a tanker for the Pacific journey to a record of almost $80 million.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche By Yongchang Chin and Nathan Risser (Bloomberg) –US crude oil exports to Asia are set to hit multi-year lows after the Iran war disrupted global shipping and pushed the cost to lease a tanker for the Pacific journey to a record of almost $80 million. Asian refinery orders for US crude for delivery in November tumbled roughly 50% to 24 million to 26 million barrels this month sequentially, according to traders who asked for anonymity because they weren’t authorized to publicly comment. If that pace of orders holds through the end of this month, it would mark a seven-year low, based on ship-tracking data from Kpler and Vortexa. The tanker rate along the US Gulf Coast-to-China route has more than tripled since the US-Iran conflict erupted in late February to almost $60 million as of Thursday, according to Baltic Exchange figures. Earlier in the month, it touched $79.6 million, an unprecedented ruction in a market where rates averaged less than $8 million in the half decade before the conflict. As it stands, leasing the largest class of crude carriers for the 30-day voyage is equivalent to half the cost of building a brand-new vessel. Those eye-watering rates doesn’t include the cost of the oil itself, which is trading around $100 a barrel. Cost to Ship US Oil to Asia Has Never Been Higher “The main story right now in the market is freight rates,” Randy Hawkins, Valero Energy Inc.’s head of oil trading, said during as conference call with analysts. Tanker rates are so inflated that refiners are effectively spending $30 to $35 to haul each barrel of crude from the Gulf Coast to Asia, or as much as seven times what they shelled out last year, Hawkins said. IEA: Gulf Oil Shipping Costs Top $37 Per Barrel, Five Times Pre-War Levels To be sure, the end of the November trading cycle isn’t a hard deadline, which leaves some leeway for traders to snap up last-minutes cargoes. At least one market participant who asked to remain anonymous said Asia-bound US cargoes for November may recover to as much as 40 million barrels in post-cycle trades. Vortexa, however, is skeptical that such a turnaround is imminent. “We don’t currently see evidence of a near-term surge that would push those volumes significantly higher,” said Rohit Rathod, a senior Vortexa analyst. The drop in Asian demand appears to be rippling across US crude pricing. Export-bound Permian Basin oil was trading for 25 cents above the benchmark futures contract at the Magellan East Houston hub as of Wednesday, down from more than $3 six weeks earlier, according to Link Data Services. Medium sour export grade Mars, which is pumped from deepwater wells in the Gulf of Mexico and is similar to Middle Eastern crude, has seen its premium to futures plunge to $6 from $17.50 in late March. US Oil Exports Surged to Record High This Year | The US sent over 6 million barrels of oil abroad each day in late April as war curtailed flows from the Middle East Valero’s Hawkins said one factor hindering global tanker availability has been the increased use of smaller vessels to pick up crude in the Persian Gulf that are less likely to be hit by Iranian fire in Strait of Hormuz. Once they’ve traversed the waterway, their cargoes are transferred to larger vessels waiting in the Gulf of Oman. “The inefficient process of this ship-to-ship transferring that they’re doing of crude oil in the Gulf of Oman is really tying up global shipping and to require more tankers to move the same amount of oil,” Hawkins said. Insurance rates and high fuel costs also are driving up freight costs, he added. “The primary factor remains high freight costs, which continue to squeeze arbitrage economics for long-haul routes,” Vortexa’s Rathod said. “The incentive for Asian buyers to source from the US Gulf Coast has diminished.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: A tanker carrying Russian diesel is expected to arrive in Norfolk, Virginia, on November 2, potentially becoming the first such shipment to reach the United States in more than three...

A tanker carrying Russian diesel is expected to arrive in Norfolk, Virginia, on November 2, potentially becoming the first such shipment to reach the United States in more than three years. The Vietnamese-flagged PVT Azura (IMO 9423683), reportedly carrying 109,000 barrels of Russian diesel, departed St. Petersburg on October 15 and is currently signaling Norfolk as its destination, according to VesselFinder . The arrival would come five days ahead of another Russian diesel shipment identified by Reuters on Friday as the first cargo heading to the United States under a recent agreement between President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Reuters reported that the Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes loaded 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low-sulfur diesel, equivalent to approximately 300,000 barrels, at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22. The tanker has signaled New York as its destination, with an expected arrival date of November 7, although its final discharge port has not been confirmed. The two shipments come as the Trump administration moves to ease restrictions on Russian diesel in an effort to bring down soaring fuel prices ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. On October 9, Trump announced an agreement under which Russia would immediately supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter. The same day, the U.S. Treasury Department issued General License 135 , authorizing transactions involving the sale, delivery, offloading and importation of Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027. On October 16, one day after the PVT Azura departed St. Petersburg, Trump also signed an executive order waiving sanctions and tariffs under the Graham Act. Trump said the waiver was “in the national interests of the United States.” The shipments would mark a rare return of Russian diesel to American ports following the Biden administration’s 2022 ban on Russian energy imports. According to the Associated Press, the last delivery of Russian diesel to the United States occurred in July 2023. The PVT Azura is a conventional product tanker owned by PetroVietnam Transportation Corporation, according to classification records, with a history of transporting Russian petroleum products. According to MyShipTracking.com, the vessel has called at several ports this year, including St. Petersburg and Svetly in Russia, the José Terminal in Venezuela, Constan?a in Romania, Szczecin in Poland, and Botlek, a major petroleum storage hub in the Port of Rotterdam, Netherlands. On February 15, the PVT Azura suffered engine failure and went adrift in Germany’s Kiel Canal. Two tugs responded and towed the tanker back toward Kiel, but sanctions related to Russian oil shipments reportedly prevented it from berthing at a German port. The tanker is reportedly not headed to the Port of Virginia’s commercial terminals in Norfolk, but instead to a facility associated with U.S. military operations. The precise discharge location and intended use of the cargo have not been independently confirmed. The U.S. Coast Guard did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication. “This effort shows other players in the oil industry that the U.S. is open for business when it comes to buying Russian diesel,” said Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. The arrival of the PVT Azura would provide an early test of the administration’s decision to reopen the U.S. market to Russian diesel, even as questions remain over how much additional supply Moscow can deliver and whether the shipments will meaningfully reduce fuel prices.
