articles.body: Brent Crude Prices Reach Five-Month High Amidst Continued Houthi Attacks, UAE Oil Spill Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Аня Крамарова Oil prices rose on Friday, with Brent crude touching its highest since early May, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East where UAE authorities also reported an oil spill . Brent crude futures gained $1.71, or 1.5%, to $114.99 a barrel by 1300 GMT, having earlier reached $115.16, the highest level since May 4. US West Texas Intermediate crude gained $1.80, or 1.8%, to $101.27. The Brent benchmark is on track for a 4.4% weekly rise, its third in a row, while WTI is poised to finish 0.4% down on the week. Saudi Aramco on Thursday ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported, as fighting intensified between the world's largest crude exporter and Yemen-based Houthis. An oil spill from a tanker was detected off the UAE coast of Umm Al Quwain, the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday. It did not say what caused the spill and authorities have not identified the tanker involved. Shipping sources said on October 9 that the Gem No.2 was struck by an unidentified projectile 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera in the UAE. "The market remains concerned about a potential escalation, which, in a worst-case scenario, could trigger renewed supply disruptions," said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo, adding that volatile oil flows and elevated freight rates have left the market undersupplied. Clashes between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government have raged since the Iran-aligned Houthis pushed towards Bab el-Mandeb last month, a shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea. In Libya, an oil pipeline valve from the Hamada and Tahara oilfields to Zawiya port has been shut, leading to a reduction in production at both fields, the head of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on Thursday. Meanwhile, the first Russian diesel bound for the US since an export agreement between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday. Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of US midterm elections on November 3. (Reuters)

articles.summary: South Korea’s push to help rebuild the American shipbuilding industry is moving beyond investments in existing shipyards and toward the development of entirely new production capacity. The latest example comes...

HD Hyundai Heavy Industries/Handout via REUTERS/File Photo South Korea’s push to help rebuild the American shipbuilding industry is moving beyond investments in existing shipyards and toward the development of entirely new production capacity. The latest example comes from HD Hyundai, one of the world’s largest shipbuilders, which has announced plans to develop a new U.S. shipyard in partnership with American engineering and construction giant Kiewit. The proposed joint venture, HD Kiewit Shipbuilding, would combine South Korean shipbuilding technology with American engineering, fabrication and construction expertise. The companies are targeting construction beginning in 2027, with full-scale operations by 2029 and the potential to create up to 3,000 jobs. But the significance extends beyond another planned shipyard. The project represents a potentially important step in South Korea’s $150 billion commitment to rebuilding U.S. shipbuilding capacity under the Make American Shipbuilding Great Again, or MASGA, initiative. It also highlights two different approaches emerging among South Korea’s shipbuilding giants: Hanwha is investing heavily in expanding an existing American shipyard, while HD Hyundai is pursuing an entirely new production facility built around modern manufacturing technology. HD Hyundai and Kiewit first announced a strategic partnership in July, laying the groundwork for cooperation on U.S. shipbuilding projects, including the fabrication of ship blocks and modules. The latest agreement takes that relationship considerably further. Rather than simply supplying technology or helping modernize existing facilities, the companies envision a purpose-built shipyard on an existing industrial site with deepwater access to the Gulf of Mexico. Although the companies have not formally identified the location, Kiewit already operates a major offshore fabrication complex in Ingleside, Texas, near Corpus Christi, where it has spent decades constructing large offshore energy structures. The facility has the waterfront access, heavy industrial fabrication experience and infrastructure needed for major marine construction projects. Kiewit has previously fabricated enormous offshore production modules there, including the 35,000-ton topsides for Shell’s Appomattox platform. The companies signed their initial shipbuilding partnership agreement at Kiewit’s Ingleside headquarters in July. For HD Hyundai, the attraction is clear. Kiewit brings established U.S. industrial capabilities, while Hyundai brings the vessel design expertise, production systems and shipyard management experience developed through decades of building ships at scale in South Korea. The companies intend to introduce HD Hyundai’s “Future of Shipyard” model, which incorporates digital twins, automated production systems, robotic welding and other advanced manufacturing technologies intended to improve productivity and reduce costs. That approach could be particularly important in the United States, where labor shortages, aging infrastructure and production inefficiencies have contributed to some of the world’s highest shipbuilding costs. The venture is initially targeting U.S. Navy auxiliary vessels, commercial ships and the fabrication of ship blocks and modules for other American shipbuilders. The latter could prove especially important. Supplying prefabricated sections to existing yards would allow the venture to contribute to U.S. shipbuilding programs without necessarily waiting for an entire vessel construction program of its own. The HD Hyundai–Kiewit project is the latest in a series of increasingly ambitious moves by South Korean shipbuilders to establish a permanent presence in the United States. Hanwha got an early start with its $100 million acquisition of Philly Shipyard in 2024, becoming the first major South Korean shipbuilder to take ownership of an American shipyard. In August 2025, Hanwha unveiled a $5 billion infrastructure plan aimed at transforming the Philadelphia facility into a high-volume production center. The plan includes additional docks, new quays, expanded block assembly capacity and advanced manufacturing technology. Hanwha has set an ambitious goal of increasing annual production from fewer than two vessels to as many as 20. The company has also begun building a commercial order pipeline, including plans for 10 Jones Act-compliant product tankers and LNG carriers, while pursuing opportunities in U.S. naval construction. HD Hyundai, meanwhile, has been building its own network of American partnerships. In July, it signed an agreement with Fraser Industries to explore shipyard modernization, including integrated design, production and management systems. Other South Korean shipbuilders are pursuing similar arrangements. Samsung Heavy Industries has established partnerships involving advanced shipbuilding technology, automated production and workforce training, while Hanwha Ocean has expanded its cooperation with U.S. defense and engineering companies. Those agreements gained additional momentum in July with the launch of the Korea–U.S. Shipbuilding Partnership Center in Washington, D.C. The center was established to coordinate investment, technology transfer, workforce development and industrial cooperation under the $150 billion MASGA initiative, which emerged from the broader U.S.–South Korea trade agreement reached in 2025. Its opening was accompanied by 15 agreements involving shipbuilders, technology companies, research institutions and other organizations from both countries. The proposed Hyundai–Kiewit yard offers one of the clearest examples yet of how that cooperation could translate into new industrial capacity. The investments are arriving at a time when the gap between American and Asian shipbuilding capacity remains enormous. According to new BIMCO analysis , Chinese shipyards now control 64% of the global shipbuilding order book, compared with 19% for South Korea and 6% for Japan. China also secured 74% of the compensated gross tonnage contracted worldwide over the past year, further strengthening its dominance across major commercial vessel sectors. The figures illustrate the scale of the challenge facing Washington as it attempts to restore domestic shipbuilding capacity after decades of decline. The United States is not starting from the same industrial position as its Asian competitors. South Korean and Chinese shipyards benefit from mature supplier networks, experienced workforces, established production systems and the economies of scale that come from building large numbers of ships. Rebuilding those capabilities in the United States will require more than new docks and modern equipment. An April report from the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that American Navy and Coast Guard shipbuilding programs have consistently suffered from cost overruns and delivery delays, with workforce shortages and infrastructure constraints among the major contributing factors. The report also warned that efforts to expand naval and commercial shipbuilding could increase competition for many of the same skilled workers and suppliers. That makes the involvement of established industrial contractors such as Kiewit particularly noteworthy. Unlike a traditional shipbuilder entering a new market, Kiewit already has an American workforce, complex fabrication experience and relationships across major industrial supply chains. Combined with HD Hyundai’s advanced production methods, those capabilities could offer a more practical starting point for expanding American shipbuilding than attempting to create an entirely new industrial operation from scratch. Still, significant questions remain about the proposed venture. HD Hyundai and Kiewit have not disclosed the project’s expected investment cost, identified the final shipyard location, announced construction contracts or provided production capacity targets. The proposed 2029 opening also leaves a relatively narrow window to develop a facility capable of undertaking complex commercial and naval construction. And while the companies have identified naval auxiliaries and commercial vessels as potential markets, neither has announced specific vessel orders for the new yard. That distinction matters. New shipbuilding capacity will only be sustainable if it is supported by a dependable pipeline of orders, a competitive cost structure and a workforce capable of maintaining production schedules. For Washington, the challenge is to ensure that the growing number of international partnerships becomes a durable American industrial base rather than a collection of high-profile investment announcements. For South Korea, the opportunity is substantial. American shipbuilding ambitions could create a long-term market for Korean technology, engineering expertise and industrial investment, while helping strengthen ties between two major maritime allies. The proposed HD Hyundai–Kiewit venture is another indication that the relationship is moving from government-level commitments toward concrete industrial projects. Whether those projects can deliver ships competitively, on schedule and at the scale Washington hopes to achieve will ultimately determine how much of America’s shipbuilding revival becomes reality. articles.title: Strait of Hormuz Ship Attacks Reach New High in October
articles.summary: October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017."October…
articles.body: Strait of Hormuz Ship Attacks Reach New High in October Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 © Adobe Stock/S.Gvozd October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017. "October has seen the highest number of ship attacks on record," said Noam Raydan, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. Raydan, who maintains the institute's interactive shipping incident map, has recorded 28 confirmed and reported attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways in October and 113 since the US-Israeli war with Iran began on February 28. The institute's map shows most of the attacks that took place in September and October were in the Strait of Hormuz. AROUND 3.5% OF WORLD SUPERTANKER FLEET ATTACKED The tally broadly aligns with data from the International Maritime Organization (IMO), which recorded a total of 120 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East since the conflict with Iran began. The IMO lists more than 30 supertankers, or Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs), that were damaged during the attacks, including 11 in October alone, a Reuters review of the IMO list and MarineTraffic vessel data showed. Each VLCC can carry about 2 million barrels of crude. The listed vessels account for about 3.5% of the total global VLCC fleet, which exceeds 900. More tankers came under attack as shipowners became increasingly willing to load cargoes inside the Gulf, lured by daily freight rates exceeding $1 million and steeper discounts offered by regional producers against dated Brent. "October 2026 has emerged as the most intense period of maritime attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the escalation of hostilities in March," Greece-based consultancy Marisks said. Between October 5 and October 11, a dozen ships were attacked, marking also the highest weekly number of attacks since the conflict began, it also said. NOT ALL ATTACKS MAY BE CAPTURED IN DATA By intensifying attacks, Iran is seeking to slow the recovery in shipments and maintain pressure on global energy markets ahead of November's US midterm elections, Raydan said. Earlier this month, Reuters reported about Tehran adopting such tactics, citing two senior Iranian officials. UKMTO, the British maritime security service, which recorded 135 incidents related to the US-Iran conflict as of October 16, said it was struggling to capture the whole picture due to insufficient voluntary reporting by shippers. The UKMTO data also showed a sharp rise in ship damage caused by attacks in October. articles.title: First Russian Diesel From Putin-Trump Deal Heading for US
articles.summary: The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday.

Join the leading maritime news network By Igor Karasi / Shutterstock Oct 23 (Reuters) – The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday. Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of November 3 US mid-term elections. Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Russia and threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless countries released more from their emergency reserves to help ease prices. The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulfur diesel in Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to LSEG shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the United States on November 7. The identity of the buyer and seller were not immediately known. The cargo will be the first imported by the US since former President Joe Biden announced a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022. Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” A Kremlin spokesperson on Friday confirmed a first ship under the deal had departed, but did not specify whether it was bound for the US market or elsewhere. “As far as I’m aware, there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy that the first tanker has, in fact, set sail for its recipients, its buyers. Further shipments will continue at a steady pace from here on,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on a daily conference call. The deal with the US involved Russia lifting a self-imposed ban on diesel exports. RUSSIA RESUMING GLOBAL EXPORTS Since the EU imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Turkey and Brazil, as well as to African countries. It also supplies Central Asia by rail. Shipping data from LSEG and Kpler published this week showed Russian diesel cargoes resuming voyages to their traditional destinations after Moscow lifted its own ban, with at least two tankers signaling trips to Turkey and Brazil. It was unclear where other tankers were destined for, with cargoes loaded in Primorsk signaling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port-Said, LSEG data showed. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said additional US shipments would follow as companies from the two countries work out the necessary contracts. Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who also heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, said last week that the US Treasury had asked the fund to help sort out tricky payment issues relating to the agreement. Novak has said that Russia would be able to increase its diesel exports to its usual levels of 3-3.5 million tons per month by year-end. articles.body: U.S. Navy Secretary Visits Fincantieri Wisconsin Shipyards Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao visits Fincantieri shipyard in Wisconsin. Image courtesy Fincantieri Fincantieri hosted Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao and senior federal officials at its Marinette and Sturgeon Bay shipyards in Wisconsin, highlighting investments in advanced manufacturing, automation and expanded shipbuilding capacity as the company prepares for construction of the U.S. Navy's Landing Ship Medium (LSM) vessels . The delegation included Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, Maritime Administration Administrator Stephen Carmel, OMB Associate Director for Shipbuilding Jerry Hendrix and Eugenio Santagata , General Manager of Fincantieri's Naval Vessels Division. George Moutafis, CEO of Fincantieri Marine Group, and Jan Allman, CEO of Fincantieri Marinette Marine, outlined the company's shipbuilding programs, capital investments and efforts to accelerate production. At Marinette, officials toured the automated panel production line and observed demonstrations of collaborative robots, augmented and virtual reality tools, and powered air-purifying respirators. Fincantieri is integrating these technologies to improve production efficiency and worker safety. At Sturgeon Bay, the delegation reviewed the shipyard's capabilities and its role in supporting simultaneous construction of multiple vessel classes. "This vital federal investment allows us to modernize" is not part of this release; instead, Moutafis emphasized the company's investments in workforce capabilities and advanced technologies to increase production rates and meet Navy requirements. The visit comes as Fincantieri Marinette Marine prepares to begin construction of four LSM vessels for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, subject to negotiations with program manager TOTE Services. In April, the Navy awarded Fincantieri an initial $30 million contract for procurement of critical materials associated with the LSM program. "Our Navy needs more skilled professionals like those I had the opportunity to meet today in order to remain the strongest Navy in the world," Cao said. The Wisconsin facilities are positioned to serve as the industrial center for Fincantieri's LSM work, expanding their role in the U.S. naval shipbuilding industrial base. articles.body: 18th Tug Delivered by Sanmar Shipyards to SAAM Towage Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 © Sanmar Shipyards Sanmar Shipyards has delivered SAAM XIMBAL, a new BOGAÇAY Class tug, to SAAM Towage, marking the 18th SANMAR-built tug delivered to the towage operator since 2018. Known as BOGAÇAY XCVI during construction in Türkiye, SAAM XIMBAL will operate from the Port of Lázaro Cárdenas on Mexico's Pacific coast, supporting demanding ship-handling operations at one of the country's major commercial ports. SAAM XIMBAL is based on the RAmparts 2400SX-MK|I design, developed exclusively for SANMAR by Canadian naval architects Robert Allan Ltd. The latest delivery brings the number of BOGAÇAY Class tugs in the SAAM Towage fleet to 13. Powered by two CAT 3516E main engines, each producing 2,350 KW at 1,800 rpm, SAAM XIMBAL combines high performance with environmentally responsible operation. A high level of onboard automation supports operational efficiency, while a sewage treatment unit and oily water separator further reduce the vessel's environmental impact as per SAAM sustainability requisites With an overall length of 24.4 meters, a molded beam of 12 meters, a least moulded depth of 4.5 meters and a navigational draught of 5.45 meters, SAAM XIMBAL combines compact dimensions with the power required for demanding harbor operations. The tug delivers over 80 tonnes of bollard pull and achieves a free-running speed of 13 knots. It is also equipped with FiFi 1 firefighting capability, further enhancing its operational versatility. SAAM XIMBAL joins a diverse group of SANMAR-built vessels already operating in the SAAM Towage fleet. Alongside the 13 BOGAÇAY Class tugs, these include three all-electric ElectRA harbor tugs and two powerful BIGAÇAY Class RAstar 29005X tugs.

articles.body: NOIA Launches Ocean Minerals Initiative Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 Courtesy NOIA The National Ocean Industries Association (NOIA) has launched Ocean Minerals Forward, a new industry education and communications initiative examining the potential of deep-sea mineral resources to strengthen U.S. critical mineral supply chains, support domestic manufacturing and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers. The initiative includes a dedicated website, a comprehensive report and educational resources covering seabed mineral development, offshore technologies, environmental considerations and the regulatory challenges facing the emerging industry. Critical minerals including nickel, cobalt, copper, manganese and rare earth elements are increasingly important to defense systems, advanced manufacturing, energy infrastructure and digital technologies. With global processing and refining capacity concentrated in a limited number of countries, NOIA argues that ocean mineral resources could complement terrestrial mining, recycling and imports from allied nations. “America cannot afford to remain dependent on foreign-controlled supply chains for the minerals that power our economy and national defense,” said NOIA President Erik Milito. “The ocean holds significant mineral resources, and companies across the U.S. and allied nations are bringing the technology, offshore expertise, and investment needed to unlock their potential.” A central theme of the initiative is the potential application of existing offshore oil and gas industry capabilities to seabed mineral exploration and recovery. Click here to download the full report. NOIA points to decades of experience in deepwater operations, including subsea robotics, autonomous underwater vehicles, geophysical surveying, dynamic positioning, specialized offshore vessels and environmental monitoring. These technologies could provide a foundation for future ocean mineral projects while creating opportunities for U.S. shipyards, ports, subsea contractors and equipment manufacturers. Environmental considerations are also addressed, including the potential effects of sediment plumes, impacts on deep-sea biodiversity and the need for environmental assessments, monitoring and regulatory oversight. The Ocean Minerals Forward report examines resource potential, global supply chain concentration, China's role in mineral processing, emerging collection technologies and opportunities for American offshore companies. NOIA said it plans to expand the platform with additional research, industry case studies and updates as technology, regulation and commercial opportunities develop. The initiative comes as the offshore industry evaluates the technical, environmental and economic feasibility of commercial seabed mineral recovery, an emerging sector where significant questions remain about environmental impacts, permitting and the development of viable processing and supply chains.

U.S. Navy photo by Lieutenant Tomas Jaramillo Romanian President Nicusor Dan accused Russia of escalating its attacks on NATO's eastern flank on Friday, after a drone strike sank a cargo ship off the Romanian Black Sea coast, killing at least one sailor with three still missing. Video released by Romanian authorities showed only a small part of the hull of the capsized tanker still visible above the waves as it sank. Romania's naval authority said the Comoros-flagged Khoryv, with a crew of 13 Ukrainian and Azeri sailors, had sent a distress signal 13 nautical miles off Romania's port of Constanta, just beyond Romanian territorial waters. The past two weeks have seen a sudden surge in deadly attacks on commercial ships off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, with at least seven cargo ships hit and some 30 sailors reported dead or missing. "It is part of Russia's escalation process in its war in Ukraine," President Dan told reporters, later saying the ship had been hit by a drone. NATO said on Tuesday it would send more maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones to the Black Sea. The alliance has not specified what capabilities would be sent. On Saturday, Romanian jetsshot down two of the latest generation of Russian drones over Romanian territorial waters. The vessels that have been struck lately have either been anchored near or headed towards the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea. The canal has become the primary export route for Ukraine, one of the world's biggest grain and food oil exporters, which has relied on Danube River ports and Romanian territorial watersas Russia has attacked Ukraine's own Black Sea ports. Stock Photo: Nickeo23/Shutterstock By Weilun Soon Oct 23, 2026 (Bloomberg) –A little-known South Korean shipowner dominated oil transits through the Strait of Hormuz in September, data from intelligence firms suggest, with the group’s vessels moving more barrels than the next three owners combined. Ships owned by Sinokor Group carried 105.6 million barrels of crude through the waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with global markets, an analysis of ship-tracking and other data from intelligence firms Vortexa, Equasis and Signal Group showed. That’s equivalent to almost 40% of oil making the crossing last month. The next three players — the National Shipping Co. of Saudi Arabia, also known as Bahri, the Kuwait Oil Tanker Company, and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co.’s shipping unit — accounted for a combined 97.3 million barrels during the same period, according to Bloomberg calculations based on that data. The analysis considered ownership and not vessel operators. None of the four companies replied to requests for comment. Sinokor, owned by tycoon Ga-Hyun Chung, gained prominence from the early weeks of the Iran war, having amassed a huge tanker fleet in the run up to the conflict through purchases or time charters. When Hormuz was all but closed off, those tankers were snapped up at exorbitant rates by producers who needed to load oil or risk running out of storage space and then being forced to undertake costly shutdowns. Read more: Iran War Supercharges Secretive Korean Tycoon’s Big Tanker Bet As Gulf crude exports recover to close to pre-war levels, Sinokor is still among the most active owners in the so-called shuttling trade, with its vessels taking short trips to pick up oil from inside the Persian Gulf, sail through Hormuz and then discharge at ship-to-ship transfer points in the Gulf of Oman. Its tankers have assisted in the transporting of crude from Saudi Arabia and the UAE, and more recently also dabbled in Iraq and Qatar shipments, ship-tracking data show. The vessels are expected to support construction activities at an offshore wind project off the UK’s east coast in 2027, working alongside OEG’s existing Chartwell-designed Fulmar and Furioso . The order marks the second collaboration between OEG and Diverse Marine following the delivery of the Fulmar in 2025. That vessel has since supported construction work at Scotland’s Inch Cape offshore wind farm. OEG director Leif Cooper said the Chartwell design performed better than expected, prompting the company to return to Diverse Marine for additional vessels. The Kangwinan project on the western Cape York Peninsula will add 20m tonnes of annual bauxite production...
articles.body: Dry Cargo Operations Rio Tinto targets larger capesizes in $1.9bn Australian bauxite push Adis Ajdin October 23, 2026 0 862 2 minutes read Bocimar Bocimar Mining giant Rio Tinto has approved a $1.9bn investment in a major bauxite expansion in Australia’s Queensland state, including an upgrade of its export facilities to accommodate larger capesize bulk carriers. The Kangwinan project on the western Cape York Peninsula will add 20m tonnes of annual bauxite production capacity, with first output targeted for 2029 and full production expected by 2032. The development will replace production from the ageing Andoom mine near Weipa, which is expected to reach the end of its life this decade, while also helping offset the planned closure of the Gove operation in the Northern Territory in 2029. Once fully operational, Kangwinan will lift annual capacity at Rio Tinto’s Weipa operations to around 44m tonnes, compared with current production of approximately 38m tonnes. The new mining centre will be located about 15 km southeast of Rio Tinto’s existing Amrun mine. A 15 km conveyor system will transport bauxite to expanded stockyards and the Amrun export wharf, which will be upgraded to handle larger capesize vessels. The mining group said the port expansion would improve shipping efficiency and reduce freight costs, strengthening its ability to supply overseas customers and Australian alumina refineries. Despite the larger vessels and additional mining capacity, analysts at SEB see limited upside for the capesize market from the investment. The bank noted that much of the new production will replace output from existing mines, leaving a relatively modest increase of around 6m tonnes compared with current Weipa production levels. Any additional volumes are also several years away. SEB further pointed out that shipments from Australia to China involve voyages roughly 3.3 times shorter than those from Guinea, where surging bauxite exports have been a major driver of capesize tonne-mile demand. The bank argued that additional Australian volumes could therefore work against the shift towards longer-haul Guinea-China trades, with the overall impact on dry bulk shipping likely to be negligible. Construction at Kangwinan is scheduled to accelerate in 2027, with the investment including $150m already approved for early works last year. The latest commitment follows Rio Tinto’s September agreement to acquire the neighbouring Aurukun bauxite project from Glencore and Mitsubishi, subject to regulatory approvals. The company intends to integrate the deposit into its longer-term development plans for the region, using existing and planned infrastructure. Bauxite’s growing importance to dry bulk shipping will be reflected at next April’s Geneva Dry , the world’s premier commodities shipping conference, with a standalone Bauxite Blitz session. Scheduled for April 28, the discussion will examine the expanding trade, shifting supply patterns and implications for future capesize demand. Confirmed speakers include Ernst Meyer, president and CEO of Torvald Klaveness, and Robert Haggquist, charterer and decarbonisation lead at South32. Braemar’s Derek Langston will moderate the session. articles.title: Eni, PTTEP forge JV to consolidate stakes in ADNOC’s giant offshore sour gas asset
articles.summary: PTTEP and Eni have created Seela Energies to streamline operations and combine their stakes in an ADNOC-operated concession off the coast of the UAE.
articles.body: Business & Finance October 23, 2026 · 18 hours ago Eni, PTTEP forge JV to consolidate stakes in ADNOC’s giant offshore sour gas asset PTTEP and Eni have created Seela Energies to streamline operations and combine their stakes in an ADNOC-operated concession off the coast of the UAE. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Hail and Ghasha island under construction Source ADNOC As one of the world’s largest sour gas mega-projects continues to take shape in the waters of the Arabian Gulf, two energy heavyweights, Thailand’s PTT Exploration and Production Public Company (PTTEP) and Italy’s Eni, have pooled their stakes in Abu Dhabi’s massive Ghasha concession, carving out a newly minted joint venture (JV) called Seela Energies to unlock financing, share deep technical expertise, and scale up their activities for the long haul. PTTEP MENA, PTTEP’s wholly owned subsidiary, together with Eni Abu Dhabi, has established Seela Energies, with each company holding a 50% shareholding. Each of the founders holds a 10% participating interest in the Ghasha concession project , which will now be transferred to the newly formed JV. As a result, the duo will hold an indirect 10% interest in the project. According to PTTEP, all required regulatory, governmental, and partner approvals have been obtained, and all conditions precedent have been fulfilled. “The establishment of Seela Energies strengthens the collaboration between PTTEP and Eni, enhances access to financing, builds capability, shares expertise and supports potential future mutual growth in Middle East region, in line with PTTEP’s strategy to deliver long-term value through strategic partnerships,” emphasized the Thai player. Related Articles Fossil Energy WATCH: First steel cut for mega gas project set on zero-emission ops by entwining smart tech, carbon capture, hydrogen, nuclear, and renewable power 7 min read The Ghasha concession offshore Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates, which is operated by the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), is expected to produce more than 1.8 billion standard cubic feet of gas per day and 150,000 barrels of oil and condensate per day over the long term. This concession is considered to be one of the world's largest sulfur-rich gas development projects and a cornerstone of the UAE's strategy to achieve gas self-sufficiency and support rising international export demand. The development concept encompasses multiple fields, including Hail and Ghasha , located in shallow waters. This project utilizes a series of artificial islands rather than traditional platforms to drill and manage operations while minimizing environmental disturbance. Related Articles Fossil Energy First jacket comes to slide into place at huge offshore gas project 3 min read The Hail and Ghasha project, designed with an emphasis on low-emissions technology, aims to operate with net-zero carbon emissions by integrating carbon capture with a target of around 1.5 million tonnes of CO2 per year, low-carbon hydrogen use to replace fuel gas, and relying on less-emission-intensive power sources, such as nuclear and solar. ADNOC’s partners in the Ghasha concession, aside from Eni and PTTEP, which consolidated their joint stakes under Seela Energies, involved other companies across the broader project lifecycle, including Wintershall Dea, OMV, and Lukoil. The Ghasha development is envisioned to employ smart technology across all operations, allowing operators, technicians, and site personnel remote access to the project’s operations. Aside from a fully unmanned facility, ADNOC has set its sights on artificial intelligence (AI), such as predictive maintenance, for all critical rotating equipment. A few months ago, the operator, in partnership with Eni and PTTEP, put into place a structured financing transaction of up to $11 billion (AED 40.4 billion) for Hail and Ghasha sour gas development. The UAE giant’s financing model follows a series of midstream and infrastructure transactions, including a $4.9 billion (AED 18 billion) oil pipeline partnership and a $10.1 billion (AED 37.1 billion) gas pipeline agreement. It also comes after build-own-operate-transfer (BOOT) projects, such as the $3.8 billion (AED 14 billion) project to power and decarbonize offshore operations and the $2.2 billion (AED 8.3 billion) project to deliver sustainable water supplies to onshore operations. articles.title: Fatigue, fear and the flaws in shipping’s safety data
articles.summary: Seafarer fatigue, mental health and reluctance to report mistakes should become key considerations for marine insurers, banks and investors, according to new research warning that shipping is overlooking significant commercial risks hidden in its own data. The Sustainable Shipping Initiative’s (SSI) From Welfare to...
articles.body: Finance and Insurance Operations Fatigue, fear and the flaws in shipping’s safety data Sam Chambers October 23, 2026 0 536 1 minute read Britannia P&I Britannia P&I Seafarer fatigue, mental health and reluctance to report mistakes should become key considerations for marine insurers, banks and investors, according to new research warning that shipping is overlooking significant commercial risks hidden in its own data. The Sustainable Shipping Initiative’s (SSI) From Welfare to Risk report, published yesterday, examines 68 sources spanning accident investigations, insurance claims, academic studies and seafarer surveys. It finds consistent links between crew wellbeing and safety outcomes, particularly involving fatigue, mental health and psychological safety. Fatigue emerges as the most extensively documented risk factor. The report warns that understaffing and excessive workloads encourage the falsification of rest-hour records, concealing dangerous working conditions from compliance systems. Between a quarter and a third of seafarers do not feel safe raising concerns or reporting mistakes, potentially undermining the accuracy of incident and near-miss reporting. The findings reinforce earlier research covered by Splash . A World Maritime University study published in 2024 found 64.3% of surveyed seafarers adjusted their work/rest records. Another welfare review, reported by Splash last month, found just 49% of seafarers believed their most recent vessel carried sufficient crew to work safely without excessive fatigue. Insurance claims provide further evidence of the financial implications. Gard’s latest crew claims report identifies stress, fatigue and excessive workloads as important factors in onboard injuries, while illness accounts for almost 60% of crew claims. SSI argues insurers can already incorporate welfare indicators into loss-prevention programmes and underwriting discussions, while lenders could include them in borrower monitoring. However, the organisation cautions that current evidence remains insufficient to use welfare indicators as standalone predictors of future claims, insurance premiums or investment performance. The next challenge is connecting existing welfare surveys, accident investigations, port state control findings and insurance claims at vessel and operator level, allowing the industry to quantify how poor crew conditions translate into financial losses. The incident occurred when the ship deviated from its planned course because the second officer on watch fell asleep. articles.body: Africa Dry Cargo Tankers Sierra Leone launches Chinese-backed national shipping company Sam Chambers October 23, 2026 0 2,161 1 minute read SLOSCO SLOSCO Sierra Leone has launched a new national shipping company backed by China’s Zhejiang Xiehai Group, with ambitions to develop a fleet of 50 vessels and capture a greater share of the country’s international cargo trade. President Julius Maada Bio inaugurated Sierra Leone Ocean Shipping Company (SLOSCO) at Queen Elizabeth II Quay in Freetown earlier this week. The venture is 70% owned by Zhejiang Xiehai Group, with the remaining 30% held by the state-owned Sierra Leone National Shipping Agency (SLNSA). The company plans to establish a fleet of 50 ships, with an initial phase involving 30 vessels, targeting dry bulk, liquid bulk and other cargoes. Its principal markets include Sierra Leone’s substantial iron ore and bauxite exports, alongside imports of petroleum products, grain and other essential commodities. “For far too long, we have relied on international carriers to export and import our products,” Bio said. The new venture follows the restructuring of Sierra Leone’s longstanding national shipping company into SLNSA last year. Legislation provides the national carrier with rights covering 40% of the value of the country’s import and export cargoes. SLOSCO is headed by chief executive Sui Xiao, with former BRS Shipbrokers executive Laurent Debart serving as chief operating officer. The company has established operations in Freetown, Shanghai and Geneva. The venture represents another expansion of Chinese shipping interests in West Africa, with Freetown seeking to retain more of the freight revenue generated by its international trade. articles.title: Icon Energy faces shareholder revolt over dilution
articles.summary: Nasdaq-listed Greek dry bulk owner Icon Energy is facing pressure from a significant shareholder to overhaul its capital structure and board, following accusations that repeated equity issuances have heavily diluted ordinary investors. Canada’s Hampton Financial, which holds 325,000 Icon shares representing...
articles.body: Containers Dry Cargo Europe Icon Energy faces shareholder revolt over dilution Adis Ajdin October 23, 2026 0 277 1 minute read Icon Energy Icon Energy Nasdaq-listed Greek dry bulk owner Icon Energy is facing pressure from a significant shareholder to overhaul its capital structure and board, following accusations that repeated equity issuances have heavily diluted ordinary investors. Canada’s Hampton Financial, which holds 325,000 Icon shares representing approximately 9% of the company, has disclosed a letter sent to Icon’s management demanding changes to its preferred shares, dividend arrangements and corporate governance. Hampton, led by chairman and chief executive Peter Deeb, claims Icon has raised approximately $25m through common share issuances since its 2024 flotation, while ordinary shareholders have suffered substantial losses. The Canadian investment firm has also questioned the treatment of preferred shares held by Icon’s controlling shareholder and chief executive, Ismini Panagiotidi. Hampton is proposing that Icon exchange its outstanding Series A preferred shares for a new instrument with a $20m face value, a fixed 6% cash dividend and conversion rights priced at $5 per ordinary share. It also wants a one-for-one share dividend for existing ordinary shareholders and the appointment of a Hampton-nominated director. The investor argues that these measures would address dilution concerns while preserving Panagiotidi’s control of the business. The proposals have not been accepted or implemented, and the filing does not establish that legal proceedings have commenced. Icon, established in 2023, operates three bulk carriers. The company entered the Nasdaq market in July 2024 and subsequently expanded its fleet through secondhand acquisitions. Its most recent disclosed commercial moves include fixing the 63,668 dwt ultramax Charlie on an index-linked charter extending into 2027 and acquiring a minority investment in two containership projects. The feeder investment, disclosed in June, marked Icon’s first publicly announced move beyond dry bulk shipping. Shipbroking sources have identified Zhoushan Changhong International Shipyard as the builder of the 212,000 dwt bulkers, with delivery scheduled for 2030. The reported contract is valued at approximately $78m per vessel and is understood to have been agreed last week. The order would mark Lavinia’s first move into newcastlemax newbuildings since 2013, when the company contracted six ships of this size. Those vessels remain part of the group’s dry bulk fleet. Lavinia has concentrated much of its recent bulker investment on smaller tonnage. The company booked eight kamsarmax newbuildings during 2023 and 2024 at Chinese yards, including CMI, COSCO Heavy Industry and Jiangsu New Hantong. Five have since joined the fleet, with another three scheduled for 2027. The Laskaridis group has also been expanding in crude tankers.In April, its Lavinia Tankers arm was linked to a fourth 157,000 dwt suezmax at South Korea’s DH Shipbuilding, following orders for three sisterships earlier this year. The $89m vessel extended a programme that began with two units in January before the owner exercised additional options. The tanker expansion followed earlier investments in MR product carriers at Changhong, where Lavinia is now reported to be returning for its latest bulk carrier programme.
